title: Our Favorite Glamping Spots in Sonoma County
summary:
Become one with nature while enjoying some creature comforts at these luxe glamping spots in Sonoma County.

The post Our Favorite Glamping Spots in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sleeping under the stars sounds wonderful until you remember that sleeping on the ground isn’t exactly comfortable and that hot showers are a good thing. In Sonoma County, you can have the best of both worlds — being one with nature while enjoying some creature comforts — at these luxe glamping spots.

Safari West, Santa Rosa

Consistently ranked as one of America’s best glamping spots by USA Today 10Best. Safari through Sonoma’s Serengeti, then spend the night in a luxury tent cabin on the 400-acre wildlife preserve. Overnight stays include a chorus of rare birds as your alarm clock and a continental breakfast. Book a South African-style braai (barbecue) for dinner at the Savannah Café for an additional charge. 3115 Porter Creek Road, Santa Rosa. 800-616-2695, safariwest.com

Sugarloaf Ridge State Park, Kenwood

Four permanent glamping tents are tucked away in the campground at Sugarloaf Ridge State Park in Kenwood. Each canvas tent features a queen bed, futon lounge chairs, rugs, tables, lights, and firewood. Other amenities include a picnic table, fire ring, and outdoor seating, plus 4,900 acres of pristine natural wonder including waterfalls, wildflowers, and majestic redwoods along the miles of hiking and biking trails. The park hosts guided events throughout the year, plus stargazing at the Robert Ferguson observatory. 2605 Adobe Canyon Road, Kenwood. 707-833-5712, sugarloafpark.org

Wildhaven, Healdsburg

Just steps from the Russian River, choose between safari-style canvas tents or cabins equipped with a bed, linens, heated mattress pads, towels, lights, electric outlets and heaters. Each site has a picnic table, fire pit, and access to a communal cooking area with barbecues and sinks. Guests can enjoy easy access to hiking trails, private access to the Russian River for a cooling afternoon dip or float, plus Saturdays bring morning yoga sessions and tasting events with local winemakers. 2411 Alexander Valley Road, Healdsburg. 707-283-7773, wildhavensonoma.com

Lake Sonoma, Geyserville

Camping at Lake Sonoma Recreation Area in Geyserville got an upgrade this summer when The Ranch at Lake Sonoma opened the first of 38 new glamping spots. The luxury canvas tents on wooden platforms are outfitted with full-sized beds and heaters. The second phase of tents will be safari tents from Botswana (which ranch manager Nikki Baxes describes as “showstoppers”) that are expected to be installed by late summer. Guests also have access to hot showers, flushing toilets, barbecues and fire rings, while the Ranch’s barn bar is a short walk away.

Despite the luxury trappings, there’s still plenty of wilderness to be found along the 17,000-acre park’s 50 miles of hiking trails. The highlight of Sonoma County’s newest glamping destination might be the views: sunlight sparkles on the lake by day, and at night, the absence of light pollution makes stargazing spectacular. 100 Lake Sonoma Overlook Road, Geyserville. 707-494-4449, theranchatlakesonoma.com

AutoCamp Russian River, Guerneville

At AutoCamp in Guerneville, guests can choose between staying in a sleek Airstream trailer, luxury tent, or the adorable and budget-friendly Happier Camper, with as much luxury as possible packed into its petite 42 square feet. The clubhouse features spa-style showers and bathrooms, general store, and a complimentary morning granola and coffee bar. On-site bike rentals mean Johnson’s Beach on the Russian River is an easy pedal away. Dog-friendly Airstreams are available for an extra fee. 4120 Old Cazadero Road, Guerneville. 888-405-7553, autocamp.com

River Electric, Guerneville

The Russian River area’s newest resort features 46 furnished tents with hotel-like amenities and access to a central bathhouse. The draw here is the resort’s two sparkling pools: a 60-foot round, family-friendly pool and a smaller adults-only area. The pool bar serves meals until 8 p.m., plus cocktails and snacks until 10 p.m. Stays include a continental breakfast. Although checkout is 11 a.m., guests have until 6 p.m. that day to enjoy the pool and restaurant. The resort also offers day passes to those not staying overnight. 16101 Neeley Road, Guerneville. 707-937-8915, theriverelectric.com

Dawn Ranch, Guerneville

In addition to top-tier dining and luxurious cottages, Dawn Ranch offers nine glamping accommodations near the property’s 120-year-old apple orchard from April to October for those who want a more immersive back-to-nature experience. Queen cabin tents feature private baths, while the king tents have shared bathroom facilities with luxury in mind. At the end of the day enjoy s’mores with guests at the communal campfire or at your accommodation’s private firepit. Borrow one of the resort’s Fender guitars for a sing-along before tucking in for the night. 16467 Highway 116, Guerneville. 707-869-0656, dawnranch.com

Sonoma Zipline Adventures, Occidental

Five treehouses, similar to yurts, form an aerial village in redwood treetops on the Alliance Redwoods property in west county. (There’s also a sixth similar ADA-compliant and accessible ground-level structure.) Every treehouse sleeps up to four, and stays include two zipline tours with Sonoma Zipline Adventures — one on the day you arrive and another before you depart. A gourmet dinner and hot breakfast will also be delivered to your arboreal retreat. 6250 Bohemian Highway, Occidental. 888-494-7868, sonomacanopytours.com

Salmon Creek Ranch, Bodega

Forget the tent. At Salmon Creek Ranch you can stay in a dreamy treehouse complete with heat, electricity and a bathroom. Located on a 400-acre working ranch on the Sonoma Coast, Eagle’s Nest Treehouse is accessed via a 30-foot spiral staircase. It features a queen bed, coffee machine and a wraparound deck for lounging — when you’re not hanging out with the ranch’s resident ducks, cows, goats and livestock guardian dogs. 1400 Bay Hill Road, Bodega. 707-775-9604, salmoncreekranch.com

This article was excerpted from our Ultimate Guide to Sonoma County’s Great Outdoors, originally published in the July/August 2026 issue of Sonoma Magazine.

title: This Spaghetti Squash Recipe Combines the Best of Summer and Fall
summary:
Once you’ve raked a fork through cooked spaghetti squash, there are myriad ways to enjoy the noodles. This recipe is one of our favorites.

The post This Spaghetti Squash Recipe Combines the Best of Summer and Fall appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Not long after pomegranates first appear and we can still find summer produce at our farmers markets, winter squashes reach out to connect late summer with early fall. It is a season of remarkable bounty and deliciousness.

Spaghetti squash, with its sun-like exterior and cooked flesh that shreds into slender noodles, hence its name, is perhaps the best transitional treat. Denser winter squashes require slow and somewhat lengthy cooking, but spaghetti squash can be roasted or steamed relatively quickly and a fork is all you need to extract the noodles. The taste is earthy and slightly sweet, but not as sweet as other winter squashes.

Once you’ve raked a fork through the cooked squash, there are myriad ways to enjoy the noodles, chilled or hot. Thai-inspired salad with spicy dressing makes a refreshing meal on hot days. Make spaghetti squash carbonara, a gluten-free delight without any sacrifice of flavor, or on chilly nights, fry sliced mushrooms and sausages and toss them with the “noodles.” Warm spaghetti squash with five-spice butter makes a delicious bed for roasted chicken.

But in early fall when we still have a colorful cornucopia of cherry tomatoes just begging to be plucked from their stems, combine them with spaghetti squash and tiny shrimp, then toss in a sweet-tart vinaigrette. It makes a dazzling dish to enjoy at home or at a picnic or potluck, as it travels well.

Spaghetti Squash, Cherry Tomatoes and Bay Shrimp with Honey-Pepper Vinaigrette

Serves 4

  • 8 ounces bay shrimp (aka Oregon pink shrimp)
  • 1 small shallot, minced
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • ¾ tsp. kosher salt, plus more to taste
  • 2 tbsp. sherry vinegar
  • 2 tsp. freshly cracked black peppercorns, plus more to taste
  • 2 tbsp. honey, warmed
  • ⅓ to ½ cup extra-virgin olive oil
  • 2 tbsp. shredded fresh spearmint leaves, optional
  • 5 cups (approximately) cooked spaghetti squash, lightly chilled (see note)
  • 1 ½ cups cherry tomatoes, halved if small, quartered if large
  • Spearmint leaves, optional, for garnish

Put the shrimp into a strainer set over a deep bowl or the kitchen sink to drain.

Meanwhile, combine the shallot, garlic and kosher salt in a small bowl, add the vinegar, and set aside for 15 minutes. Stir in the pepper, honey and 1/3 cup of olive oil. Taste and correct for salt, pepper and acid, adding the remaining olive oil if it is too tart. Fold in the mint, if using.

Put the spaghetti squash into a medium bowl, add the cherry tomatoes and half the vinaigrette, and use two forks to toss together gently. Tip into a shallow serving bowl or divide among four individual bowls. Top with the shrimp and spoon the remaining dressing over everything.

Garnish with spearmint leaves, if using, and enjoy right away.

Note: Steaming spaghetti squash instead of roasting in the oven results in the best flavor and light texture ideal for enjoying in these recipes. For about 5 cups, cut a 2 1/2 pound squash in half lengthwise, season lightly with salt, and set both halves, cut side up, in a broad steamer set over a pot of simmering water. Steam until the flesh about half an inch from the peel is just tender when pierced with a fork; do not overcook. Remove it from the heat and let it cool until easy to handle.

Use a grapefruit spoon or a paring knife to remove the seeds and the first thin layer of pulp. Discard it or set seeds aside to roast. Using a dinner fork, work from one end to the other to remove the flesh, which shreds itself as you pull on it. Spread it over a platter or baking sheet to cool completely and then proceed with the recipe.

title: Katie Ambrosi Shares Harvest Season Favorites in Wine Country
summary:
As the new executive director of Wine Road, Katie Ambrosi highlights the joys that have made Wine Country a desired destination for decades.

The post Katie Ambrosi Shares Harvest Season Favorites in Wine Country appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When Katie Ambrosi took over in June as executive director of Wine Road, an organization that for half a century has helped promote wine tourism in the Russian River, Dry Creek, and Alexander valleys, she stepped into a role that had been held by her predecessor for 25 years during a challenging time for the industry. The Healdsburg native, whose nickname is “Sparkles,” is focused on highlighting the fundamental joys that have made Wine Country a destination for decades.

“Everything’s changed. People are looking at wine in a different way,” she says. “People need to remember that wine tastes good and it’s fun. It’s great with food. It’s something that’s always been a part of celebrations and gatherings and everyday enjoyment. If we can remember that, it goes a long way.”

The mom of two boys — one in college, the other in elementary school — admits to being Healdsburg-centric, but did venture out of the ’burg some when it comes to sharing her favorite things about the harvest season in Sonoma County.

Ambrosi is a keen seamstress and frequently whips up dresses made from thrifted linens, including a gold number she made from a tablecloth for last year’s Sonoma County Harvest Fair celebration. “It showcases so many great things with Sonoma County wine and food all in one spot,” she says of the Harvest Fair. She’s already planning how to bedazzle her dress for the Red, White & Sparkle theme for this year’s Taste, Toast & Celebrate event, on Oct. 10. harvestfair.org

While kids can satisfy their sweet tooth going door-to-door on Halloween, Ambrosi heads to Dry Creek Kitchen for the chocolate peanut butter bar, a grown-up take that puts regular peanut butter cups to shame. “The candy bar dessert is exceptional. You have to make sure you save enough room that you’re able to eat that when you go there.” drycreekkitchen.com

Though not as well known as Geyserville’s famous holiday tractor parade, the town’s annual Fall Colors Festival is a must-do for Ambrosi. “I religiously attend. I have an orange and black full-circle skirt, so I bring my love of vintage dressing to it,” she says, explaining that her costume is tied to the festival’s classic car show. Held on the last Sunday of October, the day also includes a pancake breakfast, a scarecrow display and a pumpkin-decorating contest. visitgeyserville.com/fall-colors

Chances are good you’ll find Ambrosi stepping up to the mic at one of the many local karaoke nights. “I love to sing karaoke, so I have a personal challenge. I want to do one week where we do one song at a different spot every night in Sonoma County.” Two of her favorite haunts are on opposite ends of the county: Railroad Station in Cloverdale and Willowbrook Ale House in Petaluma. railroadstationbarandgrille.com; facebook.com/willowbrook.a.house

Attend Wine Road’s 50th Anniversary Grand Tasting

Saturday, Sept. 26, 4-7 p.m. at Foppiano Vineyards.

50 wineries pouring; local chefs will serve small bites.

Tickets: $125 available at wineroad.com

title: Feast on a Brilliant Fish Curry at Sebastopol’s Khom Loi
summary:
Blending a sweet summer heat with the beauty of an autumn leaf, Khom Loi’s fish curry was seemingly made for this in-between season.

The post Feast on a Brilliant Fish Curry at Sebastopol’s Khom Loi appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Khom Loi’s Panang Pla, or fish curry, arrives in a brilliant orange broth as beautiful as an autumn leaf and seemingly made for this in-between season. Its sweet heat may nod to the dog days of summer, but the warmth won’t leave you singed.

Salmon with crackling skin and tender, flaky flesh is bathed in a panang curry of red chile, crushed peanuts and coconut milk, with a citrusy lift that adds just enough tingle. A basket of sticky rice helps soak up every last drop of the Thai red curry.

Pro tip: Save a little room for a cooling swirl of soft serve ice cream topped with brûléed bananas, boba and berries.

7385 Healdsburg Ave., Suite 101, Sebastopol. 707-329-6917, khomloisonoma.com

title: Enjoy the Lake Life With Sonoma’s Skip Brand
summary:
As the founder of Healdsburg Running Company and president of Friends of Lake Sonoma, Skip Brand is here to welcome you to all the recreational fun around the lake.

The post Enjoy the Lake Life With Sonoma’s Skip Brand appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Skip Brand and his Healdsburg Running Company, a regional hub for runners of all stripes, deserve credit for introducing a key concept into the local lexicon: trail surfing.

“It means take the watch off, bring the dog out, and put the phone away,” Brand explains. Or, more simply, just flow: ride the landscape like a wave.

A longtime endurance athlete — he’s completed 15,100-mile runs and 22 Ironman triathlons — Brand also knows a thing or two about waves and water. He’s now in his fourth year as president of Friends of Lake Sonoma, a volunteer-run organization that supports the lake and its many recreational facilities.

“Its desire is to put as much recreation as possible into the lake,” Brand says.

In addition to hiking, running, biking and horseback riding on the many trails surrounding Lake Sonoma, the organization promotes water skiing, boat camping, stand-up paddleboarding and fishing.

Another popular activity on the typically calm lake is skurfing, as in ski-surfing: riding the wake of a ski boat on a single board that’s something like a surfboard, just shorter.

“Many of these folks that own slips out at the marina will come out for a Monday night tow, and it’s just incredible for them,” Brand says. “That’s why you have people from all over Sonoma County or further who use Lake Sonoma as the home base for their boat.”

Yorty Creek Recreation Area west of Cloverdale, with its protected waters and sandy beach, is a hot spot for mellower, more human-powered recreation like swimming, kayaking, canoeing and paddleboarding.

“Yorty has just been set up to be that local swimming hole,” Brand says, “and on any given Saturday or Sunday, the parking lot is full.”

Other visitors are partial to boat-in camping. Anyone with a kayak or small boat has direct access to more than 100 reservable waterfront campsites scattered around the lake. lakesonoma.org or recreation.gov

Skip Brand’s Lake Sonoma Picks

Favorite beach: Madrone Point

Favorite swim: Public boat ramp to marina, touch dock, and back. Nearly 1 mile. No-wake zone.

Favorite run: Anything from the South Lake Trailhead

Favorite boat-in campsite: Island View

title: Why Everyone Is Waiting in Line at Petaluma’s Stellina Pronto
summary:
Stellina Pronto packs pastries, pizza, sandwiches, coffee and a whole lot of neighborhood charm into one tiny Petaluma bakery.

The post Why Everyone Is Waiting in Line at Petaluma’s Stellina Pronto appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
You can see waiting in line for a cream bun at Stellina Pronto as a huge aggravation, or as an opportunity. Owners Katrina Fried and Christian Caiazzo see the lines snaking out of their tiny bakery as a chance to meet new friends, catch up with neighbors and groove to the daily playlist. Maybe it’s a glass-half-full thing, but no one waiting on busy mornings seems to be grumbling.

Stellina Pronto is Petaluma’s neighborhood bakery, full stop. There is almost always a wait because the pastries, pizza and coffee are worth the queue.

But the full cases of chocolate-filled cornetti, tarts, muffins, kouign-amann and cream puffs that overflow onto the counters — and drive much of the bakery’s revenue — weren’t really the original plan. Caiazzo, a former pizzaiolo at Wolfgang Puck’s Postrio in San Francisco and the owner of Point Reyes’ destination-worthy Stellina Osteria, was more interested in a wood-fired pizzeria with a few pastries and coffee in the morning.

Whether it was destiny or simply bad luck, the custom oven took nearly three years to receive final permitting. So the couple pivoted, and an Italian pasticceria was born.

Five years in, the pizza oven is finally the centerpiece of the busy kitchen, and its blistered-crust pies are among the best in the area. But the bakery that grew up around that delayed oven has become just as noteworthy.

What keeps people coming back is the Bible-thick menu, a mix of sweet, savory and very gluten-y goodies. (Yes, there are some gluten-free items, too.) Every inch of the place seems given over to food.

All that abundance is part of the experience. Stellina Pronto is a lot to take in, in the best possible way.

The vibe

On pleasant days, the screen door swings open and closed almost constantly, leading into a small shop packed with cold cases and a wide pastry counter piled with piadine, sweets and savory offerings. It’s visual mayhem, but the line gives you time to take it all in and adjust your order accordingly. The menu hangs overhead, offering a rough outline of what’s available, but you’ll want to get closer before making any final decisions. You probably didn’t know you needed a bear claw until you saw it glistening with sugar and cinnamon in the case.

Well-worn tile floors give the enclosed space a sense of history and community, although the bakery itself is a relative newcomer. Behind the counter, the back-of-house operation is a carefully choreographed dance, with every inch of the small kitchen put to use.

A handful of bistro tables sit on the sidewalk, along with a few bar stools lining the front windows. They’re the best seats in the house and rarely vacant. More likely, you’ll be taking your food to go — to the nearby park, your car or home with bags and boxes of goodies.

The food

With so many options, ordering can be a little overwhelming, so it helps to peruse the menu before you go. Once you reach the head of the line, things move quickly, and you’ll want to make sure you haven’t forgotten anything.

The Swedish-style cardamom bun, sprinkled with sugar, is a must-try, as is the brown sugar-coated morning bun. The Nutella-filled cornetto — the Italian cousin of a croissant — is another standout, along with jam-filled bombas and flaky mushroom-and-goat-cheese puffs.

Cookies are another signature. The crisp walnut-and-cinnamon oatmeal cookie is among the top sellers, while shortbread, pignoli, biscotti and New York-style black-and-whites are also worth a try.

For something more substantial, there are piadine, Italian handheld sandwiches made with folded pizza dough and filled with cheese, meat or vegetables. Go for the chicken or eggplant Parm ($20) or the mortadella ($18). One is easily shareable between two people. And take home a slice of yeasty focaccia slathered with tomato sauce and basil.

Don’t miss the cold cases lining the walls. They’re packed with entrée-sized salads — Italian chopped, panzanella, nectarine and feta, roasted beet — priced from $14 to $22, along with Italian sodas and, if you look carefully, containers of some of the best tiramisu this side of Italy. It isn’t too sweet, with layers of rich mascarpone and espresso-soaked sponge.

Pizza is a whole other beast and, in my book, worth a separate trip. Available only for takeout, these are pies worth exploring one by one.

The simple Rivertown ($23) is made with little more than mozzarella, fontina and basil, a minimalist pie with maximal flavor. The Puttanesca ($28) piles on olives, red onion, anchovies, garlic, fried capers, chiles and cheese. The classic Wolfgang ($32) is an ode to chef Puck’s California-style pizzas, topped with smoked salmon, dill crème fraîche, lemon zest, shallots, capers and, if you really want it, salmon caviar ($10).

The New Haven clam ($34) is the real deal. If you know, you know: These rarely translate well on the West Coast.

Somehow, there’s still more.

Coffee is a passion of Caiazzo’s, so naturally there is excellent coffee and espresso. The homemade chai has a spicy zing rather than the flat, bland muddle of factory-made stuff.

What insiders know

With a menu this sprawling, locals learn the rhythm of the week. Chicken pot pie is available Wednesday and Friday; stromboli Thursday; and wild mushroom or Bolognese lasagna Friday through Sunday.

There are also back-of-house names for popular pastries, including Cardi B for the cardamom bun and Puffy Muffy for the pull-apart muffins.

The price

You can get a pastry and coffee for around $10, or go big with a prosciutto, Brie and fig jam puff ($11). Pizzas run from $23 to $34, and piadine from $18 to $20.

This isn’t luxury pricing. Caiazzo is a stickler for locally sourced ingredients, and it isn’t just lip service. He goes all in on the best available ingredients, and the prices reflect both their quality and the labor that goes into each item.

Overall

Stellina Pronto is a “definitely worth it” spot that shouldn’t be missed. Its neighborhood feel, friendly staff, thoughtfully sourced ingredients and sheer abundance of very good things to eat make it one of Sonoma County’s best neighborhood bakeries.

The bakery is open from 6:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Wednesday through Monday and closed Tuesday. Pizza is available from 4-8 p.m. Wednesday through Monday. 23 Kentucky St., Petaluma; 707-789-9556; stellinapronto.com

The post Why Everyone Is Waiting in Line at Petaluma’s Stellina Pronto appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Our Favorite Places To Relax and Restore in Sonoma County
summary:
Soak in some hot springs, listen to a concert under the redwoods or go bird watching with friends at these local relaxing retreats.

The post Our Favorite Places To Relax and Restore in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Summer months are full of fun-in-the-sun recreation, from surfing the waves to shredding down a new mountain bike trail. But sometimes a little respite in nature can help calm the mind and ease tension in the body.

Here are some favorite Sonoma County spots to relax and restore outdoors.

Wellness by the Spring

Reflection comes easily at the new Shady Grove Movement and Wellness Pavilion at Morton’s Warm Springs Resort in Glen Ellen. Overlooking a newly restored section of Sonoma Creek, a project done in partnership with Sonoma Ecology Center, the open-air pavilion offers a restful spot for stretching, yoga, meditation, and contemplative thought with the soothing sounds of water burbling by.

The resort offers day-long retreats on Wednesdays and Thursdays that incorporate yoga, art, and herbalism workshops, as well as a therapeutic soak in the hot-spring-fed pools that have drawn people here for generations. 1651 Warm Springs Road, Glen Ellen. 707-833-5511, mortonswarmsprings.com

A Jubilant Song

Voices raised in song beneath a redwood canopy is its own kind of magic, like the yearly choral and multimedia concerts performed by Santa Rosa-based Acorn MusEcology. Since 2020, the 24-person group has performed bodies of work — most recently in May at Armstrong Redwoods — that pay homage to the environment.

Many of the group’s shows are held outdoors or in spaces that celebrate the outdoors. Their upcoming fall performance, “The Earth Says,” explores the life of soil with words by Wendell Berry and John Muir, among others, accompanied by original music. Previous concerts have spotlighted birds and beavers (to name a few).

The goal for co-founder Sarah Saulsbury is to raise awareness about ecological issues. “We need to take care of this planet,” she says. “Singing about it is one way to inspire that care.” acornsings.org

Acorn MusEcology Fall Concert Series

7 p.m. Friday, Sept. 25, St. Stephen’s Episcopal Church, Sebastopol

3 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 26, Faith Lutheran Church, Santa Rosa

3 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 27, Occidental Center for the Arts, Occidental

Birding for Everyone

Sitting for hours just to witness a winged creature fly by is its own special kind of meditation, and with the more than 400 bird species that call Sonoma County home for at least some of the year, there are plenty of opportunities to achieve some ornithological bliss. Sure, there’s the Merlin app to help with identification, but if getting off the grid is the goal, connecting with other like-minded bird nerds might be just the ticket.

The Madrone Audubon Society, a local chapter of the national organization, hosts free monthly outings for all comers. Or check out the Feminist Bird Club of Sonoma County, a group providing a safe space in the outdoors for LGBTQ+ individuals, BIPOC, and women. If you want a bespoke bird outing, Teresa and Miles Tuffli of I’m Birding Right Now offer private sessions as well as public events through Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods and the Laguna de Santa Rosa foundation. madroneaudubon.org, instagram.com/fbc.sonoma, imbirdingrightnow.com

title: Two Sonoma County Campsites Among Hipcamp’s Best in the U.S.
summary:
The 2026 Hipcamp Awards highlighted two Sonoma County campsites among the best in the nation. Here's where to book your next tent stay.

The post Two Sonoma County Campsites Among Hipcamp’s Best in the U.S. appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Campsite booking platform Hipcamp has released its guide to the “Best Places to Camp in the U.S.,” highlighting campgrounds across the country based on booking data and guest reviews.

The guide, part of Hipcamp’s annual awards, includes two Sonoma County destinations: Finley Camp and Salmon Creek Ranch, both near Bodega Bay.

Hipcamp analyzed bookings and reviews from more than 500,000 campsites for the guide, which is categorized by state and camping type. The roundup also includes two Mendocino County properties, Waterfall Camp and The Oak Show.

Finley Camp, Salmon Creek Ranch and Waterfall Camp were also featured in the 2025 Hipcamp Awards.

Finley Camp

Surrounded by Douglas firs and California bay trees, Finley Camp sits along Finley Creek, about 20 minutes from Bodega Bay. The property has 13 campsites for tents and RVs, with space between sites for privacy.

Each site has a picnic table and fire pit with a cooking grate. Wood fires are prohibited at Site 8 because it sits beneath a tree canopy. All sites have access to portable toilets and a hand-washing station.

Finley Camp is part of an active cattle ranch. Guests can contact the camp host for a price sheet for grass-fed beef or find one at the firewood stand near Site 1. The camp also offers orchard tours, during which guests can pick seasonal apples, pears and blueberries.

Well-behaved dogs are allowed but must be kept on a leash while on the property.

Rates start from $95 per night. Reservations are available through Hipcamp. To respect the host’s privacy, the exact address is provided after booking.

Salmon Creek Ranch

Located on the edge of Bodega, Salmon Creek Ranch encompasses 400 acres of redwood groves and rolling hills. The property has eight private campsites, including a secluded treehouse built by the former owners and updated by a master craftsman in 2016.

In addition to being named one of the best camps in California this year, Salmon Creek Ranch was also named among Hipcamp’s best glamping spots.

The Eagles’ Nest Treehouse has been featured in numerous magazines as a unique glamping stay perched among towering trees. Accessible by a spiral staircase and 40-foot suspension bridge, the treehouse includes a queen-sized bed with linens, potable water, a flush toilet, a copper-lined shower, a heater and an electric coffee maker.

Outside, there is a picnic table and fire pit, with barbecue utensils provided. The treehouse comfortably sleeps two people, or up to four with an additional fee.

The regular, widely spaced tent and RV sites include a picnic table and fire pit with a grill. Portable toilets are nearby, but there are no electrical hookups or potable water, so guests are advised to bring water for their stay.

The campsites sleep up to six or eight people, depending on the site, with an additional fee for extra guests.

The campground doubles as a working ranch, and a farm store on the property sells grass-fed beef, sausages and duck eggs. Well-behaved pets are welcome but must be kept away from the working ranch dogs the guard livestock.

Rates start at $120 per night. Reservations are available through Hipcamp. 1400 Bay Hill Road, Bodega, 707-775-9604, salmoncreekranch.com

title: Sonoma County’s Best Late Night Restaurants
summary:
Sometimes hunger calls after hours. Here's a helping of local spots to satisfy your late-night munchies.

The post Sonoma County’s Best Late Night Restaurants appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County has a well-earned reputation for being sleepy. Sidewalks roll up around 9 p.m. (or earlier on weekdays) and most of us head to bed. But a growing number of restaurants are staying open late for the night owls among us.

From ice cream to carnitas and blinged-out bars, we’ve got you covered.

Santa Rosa

Belly Left Coast Kitchen: Big entrees for one and small plates for sharing from celebrity chef Gray Rollin. One of the best tap selections in town. Open until 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. 523 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-526-5787, bellyleftcoastkitchenandtaproom.com

Delicias Elenita: A favorite Roseland taco truck that always has a line for their killer carnitas and elotes. Open until 1 a.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 3 a.m. Friday and Saturday. 816 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, 707-575-7021, deliciaselenita.shop

Goose & Fern: Casual British pub with excellent fish and chips, Guinness beef pie and plenty of pints. Open until 10 p.m. Sunday, Wednesday and Thursday and until 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Food is served until 9 p.m. Closed Monday and Tuesday. 116 Fifth St., Santa Rosa, 707-843-4235, thegooseandfern.com

Haku Sushi: A sibling restaurant to Han Bul with creative sushi and bento boxes. Open until midnight daily. 518 Seventh St., Santa Rosa, 707-541-6359, hakusushisantarosa.com

Han Bul Korean BBQ: Top-notch Korean barbecue at your table, plus classic dishes like bulgogi and bibimbap. Open until midnight daily. 522 Seventh St., Santa Rosa, 707-919-3094, hanbulkoreanbbq.com

Jackson’s Bar and Oven: A favorite after-work bar and up-market pub to see and be seen. Open until 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. 135 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-545-6900, jacksonsbarandoven.com

In N Out: You can get a Double-Double until 1 a.m. daily. Locations in Santa Rosa, Rohnert Park and Petaluma. in-n-out.com

NY Pie: Craving a slice past bedtime? NY Pie has you covered for late-night dine-in or delivery. Open until 11 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until midnight Friday and Saturday. 65 Brookwood Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-526-9743, nypie.pizza

La Rosa Tequileria: Modern Mexican with plenty of tequila and mezcal to wash down the never-ending tortilla chips. Open until 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. 500 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-523-3663, larosasantarosa.com

Russian River Brewing: Folks line up for their nationally recognized beers. The Santa Rosa and Windsor brewpubs have menus full of appetizers, salads, sandwiches, burgers and pizza. Both locations are open until 10 p.m. daily (last call for food at 9 p.m.). 725 Fourth St., Santa Rosa; 700 Mitchell Lane, Windsor, 707-545-2337, russianriverbrewing.com

Sebastopol

Fern Bar: Hip, modern bar and kitchen with alluring cocktails and a chef-driven menu. Open until 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. 6780 Depot St., Suite 120, 707-861-9603, fernbar.com

Screamin’ Mimi’s: If you’re jonesing for an ice cream after hours, join the line of folks with the same idea. Open until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and until 9:30 p.m. Sunday through Thursday. 6902 Sebastopol Ave., Sebastopol, 707-823-5902, screaminmimisicecream.com

Rohnert Park

Simmer Claw Bar: Vietnamese seafood meets Cajun crab boil. Prepare to get messy. Open until 10 p.m. daily. 595 Rohnert Park Expressway, Rohnert Park, 707-806-2080, simmerfamily.com

AYA: Upscale eats with a blinged-out bar and high-end wines. Restaurant open until 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and 10 p.m. Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday. Bar is open until midnight Friday and Saturday, and 11 p.m. Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday. Closed Monday and Tuesday. Bonus: The entrance is from the exterior or through the nonsmoking section. 288 Golf Course Drive W., Rohnert Park, 707-588-7115, ayasonoma.com

630 Park Steakhouse: High-class American steakhouse at the Graton Casino. Open until 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday. 288 Golf Course Drive W., Rohnert Park, 707-588-7115, gratonresortcasino.com

Petaluma

Bijou: New late-night menu and bar scene for one of Sonoma County’s most notoriously sleepy towns. On Friday and Saturday, the kitchen stays open until 11 p.m. with the full bar hopping until 1 a.m. 190 Kentucky St., Petaluma, 707-753-9155, restaurantbijou.com

Speakeasy Bistro: This hidden gem has great munchie-friendly eats, including lobster mac and cheese, wings, soft pretzels with honey-jalapeno mustard and tacos, until 11:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday, and 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday. Sister venue The Big Easy has great live music with a focus on jazz, blues and folk, with late-night hours until midnight on Friday and Saturday, and 11 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday and Sunday. 139 Petaluma Blvd. N. in the Helen Putnam Plaza, Petaluma, 707-776-4631, speakeasypetaluma.com

Sonoma

HopMonk Tavern: Brews and pub food with regular live music. Open until 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. 691 Broadway, Sonoma, 707-935-9100; 230 Petaluma Ave., Sebastopol, 707-829-7300, hopmonk.com

Healdsburg

Lo & Behold: Destination-worthy cocktails, for sure, but the creative kitchen turns out belly-fillers like chicken tenders, Korean riblets, beef brisket tacos and crispy mushroom egg rolls. A favorite late-night haunt for restaurant-industry workers. Open until midnight Thursday through Monday (kitchen closes at 10 p.m.). 214 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-756-5021, loandbeholdca.com

Roof 106: Casual upstairs bar and pizza oven at The Matheson. Open until 9 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 10 p.m. Friday and Saturday. 106 Matheson St., Healdsburg, 707-723-1106, thematheson.com

Geyserville

Geyserville Gun Club: A sibling of Diavola pizzeria, this moody bar serves up remarkable dishes and cocktails. Worth the drive. Open until 10 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and until 11:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday. 21025 Geyserville Ave., Geyserville, 707-814-0036, geyservillegunclub.com

The post Sonoma County’s Best Late Night Restaurants appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Winemaker of the Year Kara Groom Finds Success Making Wines She Likes To Drink
summary:
Kara Groom, founder of Healdsburg's Ra Ra Wine Co., was named 2026 Winemaker of the Year in the North Coast Wine Challenge for her "truly outstanding winemaking."

The post Winemaker of the Year Kara Groom Finds Success Making Wines She Likes To Drink appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When Kara Groom launched her small, independent wine label, Ra Ra Wine Co., in 2018, the fledgling winemaker never imagined she’d be named 2026 Winemaker of the Year in the North Coast Wine Challenge less than a decade later.

Raised in Sonoma County by South Australian parents, Groom didn’t plan to work in the wine industry even though her father is a respected winemaker. “I like to say I got tricked into it,” says Groom, laughing. “I was home from college and my dad told me I could earn a lot of money working harvest in Australia. I did one harvest and was immediately hooked. I fell in love with the work-hard, play-hard lifestyle.”

Today, the 34-year-old winemaker produces about 1,000 cases of wine each year for her Healdsburg-based brand, focusing on easy-drinking expressions of fresh, lively whites and less-common, lower-alcohol reds.

“I’ve always made my wine this way because it’s what I like to drink,” she says. “It just so happens people are really gravitating towards this style of wine right now, so that’s been a happy accident.”

In April, Groom entered five wines into the North Coast Wine Challenge, The Press Democrat’s annual wine competition. Little did she know she would be named Winemaker of the Year, an honor awarded to the competition’s most outstanding winemaker based on wine scores, creativity, dedication, and vision.

“There are so many amazing winemakers in Sonoma County, I’m honestly in shock I won,” says Groom, who learned of her win in July. “I’m just excited to showcase my winemaking style and the fun varietals I make because I love them so much. This is a real pinch-me moment.”

Now in its 14th year, the North Coast Wine Challenge brought together 30 local judges to blind-taste nearly 1,040 wines from 220 wineries. Eligibility was limited to wines produced with grapes from the North Coast appellation, comprising Sonoma, Napa, Mendocino, Lake, Marin, and Solano counties. Ra Ra Wine Co. earned Best Mendocino County Wine and Best of Class for its 2025 dry Gewürztraminer from Redwood Valley, plus Best of Class for its 2025 Melon de Bourgogne from Alexander Valley, and 2025 Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir Nouveau. All three wines earned Double Gold medals with scores above 95 points, with the brand also clinching gold medals for its 2025 Rosé of Grenache and 2025 dry Riesling.

“As a wine judge, I’ve evaluated countless wines over the years, and Kara’s consistently stand out for their precision, balance, and varietal authenticity,” says Jennifer Grace, president of Luxury Wine Partners. “Each wine tells a story while demonstrating technical skill and restraint, and that distinguishes truly outstanding winemaking. They aren’t simply well made — they’re memorable.”

Daryl Groom, the competition’s chief judge and Groom’s father, couldn’t be prouder of his daughter, whose wines were evaluated blind and stand on their own merit. “Kara’s wines simply delight. They’re fun and natural with no pretense — just like her personality,” says Daryl, winemaker at Naked Wines. “I am so incredibly proud of what she has done and all she has achieved.”
